themes.theme: Metrics derived from reachable-pairs-only aggregates hide disconnection — both in the optimization objective (which ends up rewarding fragmentation) and in the values surfaced to callers (which read as improved for a broken roster)
findingSummaries: penalizedAspl applies a flat +10*n penalty to any disconnected graph while ASPL is averaged over reachable pairs only, so splitting a disconnected graph further strictly LOWERS the objective; polishConstrained (and polish) therefore hill-climb into deeper fragmentation via the same flat penalty at polish.ts:39 energy() and constrainedGreedy.ts:135 constrainedMeasure, with constrainedGreedy.ts:155's guard too narrow ('was connected, now isn't') to catch it.

allPairsSummary.diameter (and aspl) are maxima/means over reachable pairs only and are surfaced verbatim as BuddyResult.diameter / ConstrainedBuddyResult.diameter, so a disconnected roster reports a small finite 'longest separation' — the opposite convention from eccentricity, which deliberately returns Infinity for the same situation.
themes.remediation: Delete the two divergent reachable-pairs-only conventions (the flat disconnection bonus in penalizedAspl/energy/constrainedMeasure, and the silently-reachable-only diameter/aspl fields) and replace both the objective and the surfaced fields with one unreachable-pair convention — e.g. count unreachable ordered pairs at a fixed value above any achievable finite distance inside the same summary used everywhere, so no code path needs its own special-cased handling of disconnection.

themes.theme: Expensive loops across the core generators (polish, ringGreedy, constrainedGreedy, fromTags) are gated inconsistently — by n alone, by an unvalidated option, by nothing, or by a check placed after the cost it's meant to bound — so several are unbounded or cliff-shaped in practice
findingSummaries: resolveWantPolish gates the 20000-iteration polish pass on n<=120 alone; per-iteration cost is O(n·m+m log m) so cost is unbounded by the gate and even non-monotone in n (120,12)=33s vs (300,12)=1s, a 300x cliff with no corresponding warning in the app.

ringGreedy has only a memory-sized cache bound (MAX_CACHED_N); its ~O(n³) time cost has no budget at all, unlike the constrained sibling which explicitly refuses the same (n,k) via MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK — validate() refuses (1000,999) while buildBuddyGraph accepts the identical input and ran 22+ minutes before being killed.

polishConstrained and polish use opts.iters/opts.maxIters directly as loop bounds with no finiteness/sign/integrality check, unlike every other numeric input in the core; JSON.parse can produce Infinity for these fields, and buildBuddyGraph/buildConstrainedBuddyGraph forward it straight into a loop that never terminates.

Constraints.fromTags takes n on faith and materializes O(n²) prohibited-pair keys before validate()'s MAX_CONSTRAINED_N check ever runs, so the size gate exists downstream of the very cost it's supposed to prevent.
themes.remediation: Remove the divergent, ad-hoc checks (the n<=120-only threshold, the absent ringGreedy budget, the unvalidated opts.iters/maxIters loop bounds, and the post-materialization n check in fromTags) and route every one of these entry points through the single work-budget guard the constrained path already has correct (MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK-style: a monotone cost model checked, and options validated, before any loop or allocation runs) instead of each maintaining its own partial gate.

themes.theme: Two functions documented as mirroring each other's precondition checks disagree on check order, so they can report a different first failure reason for the same invalid input
findingSummaries: validateDetailed() checks structural validity before size/work-budget checks, but checkWellFormed() checks size/k/work first and only calls its structural mirror (checkConstraintIds) afterward, even though the comment claims the two are kept 'in step'.
themes.remediation: Remove the divergent ordering in checkWellFormed by reordering it to call checkConstraintIds before the size/k/work checks, matching validateDetailed's actual order, rather than maintaining two independently-ordered precondition sequences.

themes.theme: Comment on a sentinel constant misstates its relationship to another sentinel, claiming distinctness where the values are identical
findingSummaries: Comment claims UNVISITED is 'distinct from' bfsDistances' UNREACHABLE but both are -1.
themes.remediation: Remove the inaccurate 'distinct from' wording and state plainly that UNVISITED is a function-scoped redefinition sharing UNREACHABLE's value, so no second definition needs to be reasoned about as if it differed.

themes.theme: Code mixes references to the original and promoted constraint object within one control-flow block, breaking the established convention of the surrounding lines
findingSummaries: Line 273 checks cons.priorCount while the rest of buildConstrainedBuddyGraph (lines 259-282) consistently uses the promoted 'active' reference.
themes.remediation: Remove the stray reference to the stale 'cons' variable on line 273 and use 'active' there, eliminating the only inconsistency rather than adding any explanatory comment.

gating.theme: once a roster is disconnected, the quality score improves as the roster gets worse, so the optimizer breaks it up further and reports better numbers
gating.summary: penalizedAspl applies a flat +10*n penalty to any disconnected graph while ASPL is averaged over reachable pairs only, so splitting a disconnected graph further strictly LOWERS the objective; polishConstrained (and polish) therefore hill-climb into deeper fragmentation, and the ASPL/diameter reported to the caller improve while largestComponentFraction collapses.
gating.failure: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(16, 2, cons) with cons prohibiting [[1,2],[12,15],[10,13],[12,13],[3,10],[12,14],[11,14],[5,11],[8,13],[7,10],[9,15],[13,15],[5,6],[2,12],[0,9],[2,13],[0,14],[6,10],[9,11],[4,10],[13,14],[8,9]] and DEFAULT options (auto-polish is on at n<=120) returns aspl=1.2777, diameter=3, report.connected=false, report.largestComponentFraction=0.25. The same call with {polish:false} returns aspl=4.9565, diameter=13, largestComponentFraction=0.875. Polish took the roster from one 14-person group to five fragments and the displayed average separation 'improved' from 5.0 to 1.3. Across 200 seeds on that instance every run ended worse than its input (best lcf reached 0.375 vs 0.875 at the start). Sibling on the unconstrained export, which has no connectivity guard at all: g = 12-cycle on 0..11 plus 4-cycle on 12..15; polish(g,{mode:'hill',seed:1,maxIters:4000}) returns 4 components (sizes 5,4,4,3), lcf 0.75 -> 0.3125, and reports aspl 1.36, connected false.
gating.remediation: Make the disconnection penalty monotone in fragmentation instead of flat, so no move that increases the number of components can ever lower the energy — e.g. penalize per stranded vertex / per extra component (aspl + 10*n*(n - largestComponentSize) or + 10*n*(components-1)), and count unreachable ordered pairs at a value above any achievable finite distance rather than dropping them from the mean. Per lib/CLAUDE.md the objective is mirrored, so change reference-python/core.py penalized_aspl (and constrained_gen.py's measure) first, regenerate fixtures, then mirror. Close the whole theme, not the reported call: the identical flat penalty is consumed by polish.ts:39 energy() (which has NO wasConnected guard, only the energy comparison) and by constrainedGreedy.ts:135 constrainedMeasure, and constrainedGreedy.ts:155's guard must be widened from 'was connected and now is not' to 'component count must never increase'.
gating.invariant: For every Graph g, every Constraints c, every seed and iteration budget: connectedComponents(polishConstrained(g,c,opts)).length <= connectedComponents(g).length AND largestComponentFraction(polishConstrained(g,c,opts)) >= largestComponentFraction(g); the same must hold for polish(g,opts).graph in both modes. Equivalently, for any two graphs on the same n, penalizedAspl must be strictly greater for the one with strictly more connected components.

gating.theme: an aggregate computed over reachable pairs only is surfaced as if it described the whole roster, so a split group reads as tighter than a whole one
gating.summary: allPairsSummary.diameter (and aspl) are maxima/means over reachable pairs only and are surfaced verbatim as BuddyResult.diameter / ConstrainedBuddyResult.diameter, so a disconnected roster reports a small finite 'longest separation' — the exact convention eccentricity's own docstring (metrics.ts:97) rejects, where it deliberately returns Infinity instead of a small finite number for the same situation.
gating.failure: For the n=16,k=2 instance above, buildConstrainedBuddyGraph reports diameter: 3 and aspl: 1.2777 for a graph in which most pairs of people cannot reach each other at all; eccentricity(g, v) on the very same graph returns Infinity for every v. The two exported metrics disagree about what 'distance to an unreachable person' means, and the one a UI shows for 'longest separation' is the one that reads as excellent.
gating.remediation: Pick one convention across the module and apply it to the surfaced fields: either return Infinity for diameter (and aspl) when summary.connected is false, matching eccentricity, or rename the fields to state the restriction (asplWithinGroups / diameterWithinGroups) and require the connectivity flag to travel with them. If the Infinity route is taken, change reference-python/core.py all_pairs_summary first and regenerate fixtures, since fixture parity currently pins the finite value.
gating.invariant: For every Graph g and every vertex v: eccentricity(g,v) === Infinity implies that every consumer-facing distance aggregate for g (allPairsSummary(g).diameter and .aspl, BuddyResult.diameter/.aspl, ConstrainedBuddyResult.diameter/.aspl) is also Infinity — i.e. the module never reports a finite 'distance' aggregate for a graph whose connectivity flag is false.

gating.theme: the polish stage's cost gate is an iteration count keyed on n alone, so the default-options cost at the threshold is tens of seconds and is non-monotone in n
gating.summary: resolveWantPolish enables a 20000-iteration polish pass whenever n <= 120, and polish's per-iteration cost is O(n·m + m log m) (a full edgeList() + allPairsSummary() re-measure). The threshold bounds n but nothing bounds the product, so the most expensive input on the entire unconstrained path sits just below the gate. Measured with default options: buildBuddyGraph(120,12) = 33.0 s (reproduced 34.0 s), buildBuddyGraph(120,4) = 18.5 s, buildBuddyGraph(121,12) = 0.1 s, buildBuddyGraph(300,12) = 1.0 s — a 300x cost cliff, and cost that DECREASES with n. This is default configuration, present-day reachable from the app: app/src/worker/generate.ts calls buildBuddyGraph(n,k,options) with polish:'auto', n up to MAX_ROSTER_N=1000 and k up to BUDDY_MAX=12, so a 120-name roster at 12 buddies runs ~33 s per generate and again per seed-bump reroll (in a worker, so the tab is not frozen — but app/src/io/feasibility.ts only warns above n>300, i.e. the slow case is exactly the one that gets no warning). It also contradicts the stated rationale: lib/CLAUDE.md justifies the n<=120 cap as what keeps polish affordable, and docs/findings/FINDINGS.md sizes polish in TIME ('thorough (8 s) polish budget'), while the shipped budget is a bare count that costs 4x that at the cap.
gating.failure: buildBuddyGraph(120, 12) with default options returns after 33.0 s; buildBuddyGraph(121, 12) returns after 0.1 s. Same k, one more person, 300x less work.
gating.invariant: For all (n, k) accepted by buildBuddyGraph, the modelled polish work under DEFAULT options — iterations × per-iteration cost, i.e. iters·n·m where m is the edge count of the seed graph — is <= one declared constant budget; equivalently, the iteration budget must be derived from that budget rather than fixed, so that default-option generation cost is monotone non-decreasing in n at fixed k (today it is not: cost(120,k) >> cost(121,k)).
gating.remediation: Make the polish budget a work budget, not a count: derive maxIters from a declared cost ceiling (e.g. iters = clamp(BUDGET / (n·m))) and gate auto-polish on that modelled work rather than on `n <= 120` alone, so density/k participate. Pin the invariant with a test asserting default-option modelled work is bounded by the constant AND monotone in n across the old threshold (n=119..122 at k=BUDDY_MAX), which fails today by construction of the cliff. Update lib/CLAUDE.md's 'auto-polish is capped at n<=120' rationale with the measured cost at the cap.

gating.theme: the unconstrained generator has no work budget, so an (n,k) the constrained sibling explicitly refuses as unrunnable is accepted and runs for tens of minutes
gating.summary: ringGreedy's only size gate is MAX_CACHED_N (5000), documented in-file as a MEMORY bound on the n×n distance cache ('~100 MB at this n'); the same comment concedes completion is ~O(n³) time and no gate bounds it. k is not bounded at all beyond k>=2. The constrained path treats this exact class as a blocking hazard — MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK + constrainedWork(n,k) exist solely to refuse dense-k rosters, with a whole findings doc (docs/findings/constrained-generation-cost-and-caps.md) explaining that the n-cap alone is insufficient — but buildBuddyGraph/ringGreedy get neither the work model nor the refusal. Measured: validate(new Constraints(1000), 999) refuses with 'roster size 1000 with 999 buddies each is too large to generate in reasonable time', while buildBuddyGraph(1000, 999, {polish:false}) accepted the identical (n,k) and had not returned after 22 minutes (killed). Same asymmetry at (5000,12): validate refuses; ringGreedy accepts (n <= MAX_CACHED_N). Sparse scaling measured at ~n³: (500,4)=0.55 s, (1000,4)=5.4 s, (1500,4)=16.8 s, (1000,12)=38.5 s, so the largest accepted sparse input (5000,12) extrapolates to tens of minutes. Present-day app reachability is bounded by app-side clamps (n<=1000, k<=12 → 38 s in a worker); the unbounded case is reachable from any direct consumer of the published package, and lib/CLAUDE.md asserts the opposite ('The generators that ARE the untrusted surface are capped (MAX_CACHED_N, MAX_CONSTRAINED_N, MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK)').
gating.failure: buildBuddyGraph(1000, 999, {polish:false}) does not return within 22 minutes; validate(new Constraints(1000), 999) refuses the same (n,k) in under 1 ms as 'too large to generate in reasonable time'.
gating.invariant: For all integer n >= 0 and k >= 0, if any generation entry point ACCEPTS (n,k) (does not throw or refuse) then its modelled work is <= that path's declared budget. In particular the accept-sets must not disagree across paths for the same cost class: there is no (n,k) that validate() refuses as 'too large to generate' but ringGreedy/buildBuddyGraph accept (ringGreedy's own model must be at least as strict, since its per-edge cost is O(n²) cache update, not O(n) BFS).
gating.remediation: Give ringGreedy a work budget in the same shape as MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK: a monotone model of its actual cost (~n²·edgesAdded ≈ n³·min(k,n-1)/2, which is worse than constrainedWork) compared against a constant in graph.ts, enforced as a throw in ringGreedy alongside the existing MAX_CACHED_N check and surfaced through buildBuddyGraph's documented throw contract. Ratchet with a property test over integer (n,k) asserting the accept-set containment above, and correct the 'the untrusted generators are capped' claim in lib/CLAUDE.md.

gating.theme: numeric fields of the options object are taken on faith while n and k are validated, so a non-finite budget becomes an unbounded loop
gating.summary: polishConstrained uses `opts.iters ?? 8000` directly as the loop bound (`for (let it = 0; it < iters; it++)`), and polish.ts:48 does the same with `opts.maxIters ?? 20000` (`while (iters < maxIters)`). Neither is checked for finiteness, integrality or sign, unlike every other numeric input in the core (n, k, and even Graph's ctor are guarded). Infinity is directly obtainable from a JSON settings object — JSON has no Infinity literal, but JSON.parse('{"polishIters":1e999}').polishIters === Infinity (verified) — and buildBuddyGraph/buildConstrainedBuddyGraph forward polishIters straight through. Verified: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(30,4,new Constraints(30),{polish:true,polishIters:Infinity}) and buildBuddyGraph(30,4,{polish:true,polishIters:1e18}) both had to be killed by timeout; the only loop exit is edges.length < 2, so with >= 2 edges neither ever terminates. This also breaks buildConstrainedBuddyGraph's documented 'refuses, never throws' contract in the worst way — it neither refuses nor returns. The same unvalidated-option class produces garbage rather than a hang elsewhere: buildBuddyGraph(20,4,{minSeparation:NaN}) returns finalMinSeparation: NaN (a numeric result field that JSON.stringify writes as null), and minSeparation:-5 returns finalMinSeparation:-5. Not reachable from the app today — app/src/worker/protocol.ts's GenerateOptions carries only minSeparation/polish/seed, and importGraph sanitizes those — hence suggestion, not blocking; it is reachable from any direct consumer of the published package.
gating.failure: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(30, 4, new Constraints(30), {polish: true, polishIters: Infinity}) never returns (killed at 10 s; the loop bound is literally Infinity). Secondary: buildBuddyGraph(20, 4, {minSeparation: NaN}).finalMinSeparation === NaN.
gating.invariant: For every exported entry point, every loop bound derived from an options object is a finite non-negative integer — a value outside that domain is refused (throw on the unconstrained path / refusal on the constrained path) or replaced by the documented default before use; consequently every call returns in work bounded by a function of (n, k) and that finite budget. Corollary for the same fix: no numeric field of a non-refused result is NaN.
gating.remediation: Validate the options object where n and k are validated: in buildBuddyGraph/buildConstrainedBuddyGraph and in polish/polishConstrained, coerce or refuse non-integer/non-finite/negative polishIters|maxIters|iters (and minSeparation) instead of using them as loop bounds. Property-test: for every entry point and every options field, a non-finite/non-integer/negative value either throws/refuses or produces the same result as the documented default, and the call completes within a bounded step count.

gating.theme: two functions that document themselves as mirroring each other's precondition checks actually check in a different order, so they can report a different *first* reason for the same invalid input
gating.summary: validateDetailed() (constraints.ts) checks structural validity (out-of-range constraint ids / self-pairs) BEFORE the size/work-budget checks and returns early on a structural hit. checkWellFormed() (constrainedGreedy.ts, the throw-based precondition for direct callers of constrainedGreedy) checks n/MAX_CONSTRAINED_N/k/MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK FIRST and only calls checkConstraintIds() (the structural mirror) afterward. The comment on checkConstraintIds says it is a 'Throw-on-first mirror of constraints.ts structuralReasons... keep the two checks in step' -- true for the id-validity logic in isolation, but the two entry points disagree on which class of problem is reported first when an input is both oversized AND structurally invalid.
gating.failure: n = 10000 (over MAX_CONSTRAINED_N = 5000) with a constraint pair referencing person 99999: validateDetailed(cons, k) returns [{code:'unknown-person', person:99999, n:10000}] (structural short-circuit fires before the n>MAX_CONSTRAINED_N check ever runs), while a direct call to constrainedGreedy(10000, k, cons) throws "roster size 10000 exceeds the constrained maximum of 5000" (checkWellFormed's n-cap check fires before checkConstraintIds runs). Same malformed input, two different 'first' diagnoses depending on which of the two documented-as-mirrored guards is asked.
gating.remediation: Reorder checkWellFormed to run checkConstraintIds before the size/k/work checks (matching validateDetailed's actual order), or state explicitly in both comments that only the *content* of the structural check is mirrored, not its priority relative to the size/work gates, so a future reader doesn't rely on 'in step' meaning identical precedence.
gating.invariant: for any (n, k, cons) that is both structurally invalid (out-of-range id or self-pair) and over a size/work cap, the Reason.code that would be first in validateDetailed(cons,k) matches the class of error thrown first by calling constrainedGreedy(n,k,cons) directly.

gating.theme: ambiguous constant relationship comment could mislead on whether values are identical
gating.summary: Comment claims UNVISITED is 'distinct from' UNREACHABLE but both are -1
gating.failure: Line 7 defines UNREACHABLE = -1; line 210 defines UNVISITED = -1 with comment 'distinct from bfsDistances' UNREACHABLE'. A maintainer reading 'distinct from' may assume they should have different values, then refactor them apart, breaking the logic. Both serve as visit-markers (same semantic function, different scopes) and sharing -1 is intentional and correct.
gating.invariant: When two constants in the same module share an identical value for valid semantic reasons, the comment must clarify the value reuse is intentional, not accidental. The word 'distinct' must not be used to describe a relationship where values are identical.
gating.remediation: Change the comment from 'distinct from bfsDistances' UNREACHABLE' to 'local redefinition of UNREACHABLE; same value (-1) but function-scoped', or 'per-source BFS marker; mirrors UNREACHABLE sentinel value'.

gating.theme: mixing original and promoted constraint references within same control flow breaks readability
gating.summary: Line 273 checks cons.priorCount; rest of buildConstrainedBuddyGraph (lines 259-282) consistently uses active
gating.failure: Function creates active = withHardPriors(cons) at line 259, then validates active (260), passes active to constrainedGreedy (263) and polishConstrained (276). But at line 273, deciding priorWeight, it checks cons.priorCount instead of active.priorCount. While functionally equivalent (active and cons have identical priors when priorHard is false), it breaks the local convention. A future maintainer modifying the promotion logic might assume the split reference is intentional and create a subtle bug.
gating.invariant: Within a single function where a promoted variant (active) is derived from an original (cons), references to the constraint set should use active consistently unless the comment explicitly justifies using the original.
gating.remediation: Change line 273 from 'cons.priorCount > 0' to 'active.priorCount > 0' for consistency with lines 260, 263, 271, 276.

confirmed.theme: once a roster is disconnected, the quality score improves as the roster gets worse, so the optimizer breaks it up further and reports better numbers
confirmed.summary: penalizedAspl applies a flat +10*n penalty to any disconnected graph while ASPL is averaged over reachable pairs only, so splitting a disconnected graph further strictly LOWERS the objective; polishConstrained (and polish) therefore hill-climb into deeper fragmentation, and the ASPL/diameter reported to the caller improve while largestComponentFraction collapses.
confirmed.failure: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(16, 2, cons) with cons prohibiting [[1,2],[12,15],[10,13],[12,13],[3,10],[12,14],[11,14],[5,11],[8,13],[7,10],[9,15],[13,15],[5,6],[2,12],[0,9],[2,13],[0,14],[6,10],[9,11],[4,10],[13,14],[8,9]] and DEFAULT options (auto-polish is on at n<=120) returns aspl=1.2777, diameter=3, report.connected=false, report.largestComponentFraction=0.25. The same call with {polish:false} returns aspl=4.9565, diameter=13, largestComponentFraction=0.875. Polish took the roster from one 14-person group to five fragments and the displayed average separation 'improved' from 5.0 to 1.3. Across 200 seeds on that instance every run ended worse than its input (best lcf reached 0.375 vs 0.875 at the start). Sibling on the unconstrained export, which has no connectivity guard at all: g = 12-cycle on 0..11 plus 4-cycle on 12..15; polish(g,{mode:'hill',seed:1,maxIters:4000}) returns 4 components (sizes 5,4,4,3), lcf 0.75 -> 0.3125, and reports aspl 1.36, connected false.
confirmed.remediation: Make the disconnection penalty monotone in fragmentation instead of flat, so no move that increases the number of components can ever lower the energy — e.g. penalize per stranded vertex / per extra component (aspl + 10*n*(n - largestComponentSize) or + 10*n*(components-1)), and count unreachable ordered pairs at a value above any achievable finite distance rather than dropping them from the mean. Per lib/CLAUDE.md the objective is mirrored, so change reference-python/core.py penalized_aspl (and constrained_gen.py's measure) first, regenerate fixtures, then mirror. Close the whole theme, not the reported call: the identical flat penalty is consumed by polish.ts:39 energy() (which has NO wasConnected guard, only the energy comparison) and by constrainedGreedy.ts:135 constrainedMeasure, and constrainedGreedy.ts:155's guard must be widened from 'was connected and now is not' to 'component count must never increase'.
confirmed.invariant: For every Graph g, every Constraints c, every seed and iteration budget: connectedComponents(polishConstrained(g,c,opts)).length <= connectedComponents(g).length AND largestComponentFraction(polishConstrained(g,c,opts)) >= largestComponentFraction(g); the same must hold for polish(g,opts).graph in both modes. Equivalently, for any two graphs on the same n, penalizedAspl must be strictly greater for the one with strictly more connected components.

confirmed.theme: an aggregate computed over reachable pairs only is surfaced as if it described the whole roster, so a split group reads as tighter than a whole one
confirmed.summary: allPairsSummary.diameter (and aspl) are maxima/means over reachable pairs only and are surfaced verbatim as BuddyResult.diameter / ConstrainedBuddyResult.diameter, so a disconnected roster reports a small finite 'longest separation' — the exact convention eccentricity's own docstring (metrics.ts:97) rejects, where it deliberately returns Infinity instead of a small finite number for the same situation.
confirmed.failure: For the n=16,k=2 instance above, buildConstrainedBuddyGraph reports diameter: 3 and aspl: 1.2777 for a graph in which most pairs of people cannot reach each other at all; eccentricity(g, v) on the very same graph returns Infinity for every v. The two exported metrics disagree about what 'distance to an unreachable person' means, and the one a UI shows for 'longest separation' is the one that reads as excellent.
confirmed.remediation: Pick one convention across the module and apply it to the surfaced fields: either return Infinity for diameter (and aspl) when summary.connected is false, matching eccentricity, or rename the fields to state the restriction (asplWithinGroups / diameterWithinGroups) and require the connectivity flag to travel with them. If the Infinity route is taken, change reference-python/core.py all_pairs_summary first and regenerate fixtures, since fixture parity currently pins the finite value.
confirmed.invariant: For every Graph g and every vertex v: eccentricity(g,v) === Infinity implies that every consumer-facing distance aggregate for g (allPairsSummary(g).diameter and .aspl, BuddyResult.diameter/.aspl, ConstrainedBuddyResult.diameter/.aspl) is also Infinity — i.e. the module never reports a finite 'distance' aggregate for a graph whose connectivity flag is false.

confirmed.theme: the polish stage's cost gate is an iteration count keyed on n alone, so the default-options cost at the threshold is tens of seconds and is non-monotone in n
confirmed.summary: resolveWantPolish enables a 20000-iteration polish pass whenever n <= 120, and polish's per-iteration cost is O(n·m + m log m) (a full edgeList() + allPairsSummary() re-measure). The threshold bounds n but nothing bounds the product, so the most expensive input on the entire unconstrained path sits just below the gate. Measured with default options: buildBuddyGraph(120,12) = 33.0 s (reproduced 34.0 s), buildBuddyGraph(120,4) = 18.5 s, buildBuddyGraph(121,12) = 0.1 s, buildBuddyGraph(300,12) = 1.0 s — a 300x cost cliff, and cost that DECREASES with n. This is default configuration, present-day reachable from the app: app/src/worker/generate.ts calls buildBuddyGraph(n,k,options) with polish:'auto', n up to MAX_ROSTER_N=1000 and k up to BUDDY_MAX=12, so a 120-name roster at 12 buddies runs ~33 s per generate and again per seed-bump reroll (in a worker, so the tab is not frozen — but app/src/io/feasibility.ts only warns above n>300, i.e. the slow case is exactly the one that gets no warning). It also contradicts the stated rationale: lib/CLAUDE.md justifies the n<=120 cap as what keeps polish affordable, and docs/findings/FINDINGS.md sizes polish in TIME ('thorough (8 s) polish budget'), while the shipped budget is a bare count that costs 4x that at the cap.
confirmed.failure: buildBuddyGraph(120, 12) with default options returns after 33.0 s; buildBuddyGraph(121, 12) returns after 0.1 s. Same k, one more person, 300x less work.
confirmed.invariant: For all (n, k) accepted by buildBuddyGraph, the modelled polish work under DEFAULT options — iterations × per-iteration cost, i.e. iters·n·m where m is the edge count of the seed graph — is <= one declared constant budget; equivalently, the iteration budget must be derived from that budget rather than fixed, so that default-option generation cost is monotone non-decreasing in n at fixed k (today it is not: cost(120,k) >> cost(121,k)).
confirmed.remediation: Make the polish budget a work budget, not a count: derive maxIters from a declared cost ceiling (e.g. iters = clamp(BUDGET / (n·m))) and gate auto-polish on that modelled work rather than on `n <= 120` alone, so density/k participate. Pin the invariant with a test asserting default-option modelled work is bounded by the constant AND monotone in n across the old threshold (n=119..122 at k=BUDDY_MAX), which fails today by construction of the cliff. Update lib/CLAUDE.md's 'auto-polish is capped at n<=120' rationale with the measured cost at the cap.

confirmed.theme: the unconstrained generator has no work budget, so an (n,k) the constrained sibling explicitly refuses as unrunnable is accepted and runs for tens of minutes
confirmed.summary: ringGreedy's only size gate is MAX_CACHED_N (5000), documented in-file as a MEMORY bound on the n×n distance cache ('~100 MB at this n'); the same comment concedes completion is ~O(n³) time and no gate bounds it. k is not bounded at all beyond k>=2. The constrained path treats this exact class as a blocking hazard — MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK + constrainedWork(n,k) exist solely to refuse dense-k rosters, with a whole findings doc (docs/findings/constrained-generation-cost-and-caps.md) explaining that the n-cap alone is insufficient — but buildBuddyGraph/ringGreedy get neither the work model nor the refusal. Measured: validate(new Constraints(1000), 999) refuses with 'roster size 1000 with 999 buddies each is too large to generate in reasonable time', while buildBuddyGraph(1000, 999, {polish:false}) accepted the identical (n,k) and had not returned after 22 minutes (killed). Same asymmetry at (5000,12): validate refuses; ringGreedy accepts (n <= MAX_CACHED_N). Sparse scaling measured at ~n³: (500,4)=0.55 s, (1000,4)=5.4 s, (1500,4)=16.8 s, (1000,12)=38.5 s, so the largest accepted sparse input (5000,12) extrapolates to tens of minutes. Present-day app reachability is bounded by app-side clamps (n<=1000, k<=12 → 38 s in a worker); the unbounded case is reachable from any direct consumer of the published package, and lib/CLAUDE.md asserts the opposite ('The generators that ARE the untrusted surface are capped (MAX_CACHED_N, MAX_CONSTRAINED_N, MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK)').
confirmed.failure: buildBuddyGraph(1000, 999, {polish:false}) does not return within 22 minutes; validate(new Constraints(1000), 999) refuses the same (n,k) in under 1 ms as 'too large to generate in reasonable time'.
confirmed.invariant: For all integer n >= 0 and k >= 0, if any generation entry point ACCEPTS (n,k) (does not throw or refuse) then its modelled work is <= that path's declared budget. In particular the accept-sets must not disagree across paths for the same cost class: there is no (n,k) that validate() refuses as 'too large to generate' but ringGreedy/buildBuddyGraph accept (ringGreedy's own model must be at least as strict, since its per-edge cost is O(n²) cache update, not O(n) BFS).
confirmed.remediation: Give ringGreedy a work budget in the same shape as MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK: a monotone model of its actual cost (~n²·edgesAdded ≈ n³·min(k,n-1)/2, which is worse than constrainedWork) compared against a constant in graph.ts, enforced as a throw in ringGreedy alongside the existing MAX_CACHED_N check and surfaced through buildBuddyGraph's documented throw contract. Ratchet with a property test over integer (n,k) asserting the accept-set containment above, and correct the 'the untrusted generators are capped' claim in lib/CLAUDE.md.

confirmed.theme: numeric fields of the options object are taken on faith while n and k are validated, so a non-finite budget becomes an unbounded loop
confirmed.summary: polishConstrained uses `opts.iters ?? 8000` directly as the loop bound (`for (let it = 0; it < iters; it++)`), and polish.ts:48 does the same with `opts.maxIters ?? 20000` (`while (iters < maxIters)`). Neither is checked for finiteness, integrality or sign, unlike every other numeric input in the core (n, k, and even Graph's ctor are guarded). Infinity is directly obtainable from a JSON settings object — JSON has no Infinity literal, but JSON.parse('{"polishIters":1e999}').polishIters === Infinity (verified) — and buildBuddyGraph/buildConstrainedBuddyGraph forward polishIters straight through. Verified: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(30,4,new Constraints(30),{polish:true,polishIters:Infinity}) and buildBuddyGraph(30,4,{polish:true,polishIters:1e18}) both had to be killed by timeout; the only loop exit is edges.length < 2, so with >= 2 edges neither ever terminates. This also breaks buildConstrainedBuddyGraph's documented 'refuses, never throws' contract in the worst way — it neither refuses nor returns. The same unvalidated-option class produces garbage rather than a hang elsewhere: buildBuddyGraph(20,4,{minSeparation:NaN}) returns finalMinSeparation: NaN (a numeric result field that JSON.stringify writes as null), and minSeparation:-5 returns finalMinSeparation:-5. Not reachable from the app today — app/src/worker/protocol.ts's GenerateOptions carries only minSeparation/polish/seed, and importGraph sanitizes those — hence suggestion, not blocking; it is reachable from any direct consumer of the published package.
confirmed.failure: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(30, 4, new Constraints(30), {polish: true, polishIters: Infinity}) never returns (killed at 10 s; the loop bound is literally Infinity). Secondary: buildBuddyGraph(20, 4, {minSeparation: NaN}).finalMinSeparation === NaN.
confirmed.invariant: For every exported entry point, every loop bound derived from an options object is a finite non-negative integer — a value outside that domain is refused (throw on the unconstrained path / refusal on the constrained path) or replaced by the documented default before use; consequently every call returns in work bounded by a function of (n, k) and that finite budget. Corollary for the same fix: no numeric field of a non-refused result is NaN.
confirmed.remediation: Validate the options object where n and k are validated: in buildBuddyGraph/buildConstrainedBuddyGraph and in polish/polishConstrained, coerce or refuse non-integer/non-finite/negative polishIters|maxIters|iters (and minSeparation) instead of using them as loop bounds. Property-test: for every entry point and every options field, a non-finite/non-integer/negative value either throws/refuses or produces the same result as the documented default, and the call completes within a bounded step count.

confirmed.theme: tag compilation materializes O(n²) pair constraints and validates nothing about n, so the size gate can never run
confirmed.summary: Constraints.fromTags takes n on faith — no Number.isInteger / MAX_ROSTER check, unlike degreeOf (same file, line 39), the Graph ctor, and validate — and then materializes one Set key per same-tag pair. Measured: fromTags(3000, Array(3000).fill('A')) takes 3.4 s and builds 4 498 500 prohibited keys; the cost is paid inside the constructor, so validate()'s MAX_CONSTRAINED_N refusal never gets a chance to run (this is the 'gate after the work it is meant to bound' shape). fromTags(2e7, []) runs a pure 2e7-iteration loop with no allocation and no guard, so a large non-integer-checked n is a straight time sink. Filed as DEFERRAL per the reporting contract: grep shows no caller outside lib/test/constrained.test.ts — the app never calls fromTags — so nothing untrusted reaches it in the current tree. The O(n²) materialization half is already tracked in lib/CLAUDE.md's known limitations ('Sanitize + size-check tags when F6 lands'); the missing n validation is not.
confirmed.failure: Constraints.fromTags(3000, new Array(3000).fill('A')) spends 3.4 s and 4.5M Set keys before any validate() can refuse; Constraints.fromTags(1e15, []) loops with no guard at all.
confirmed.invariant: Constraints.fromTags refuses an n that is not an integer in [0, MAX_ROSTER] BEFORE any loop, and refuses a tag distribution whose implied pair count exceeds a declared cap BEFORE materializing pairs — i.e. the number of Set insertions performed by fromTags is bounded by a constant for every (n, tags) it does not refuse.
confirmed.remediation: Reuse the same n guard degreeOf already has, and pre-count group sizes (one O(n) pass over tags) to compute sum(size·(size-1)/2) and refuse against a declared pair cap before the double loop. Defer until a caller exists; keep it in the known-limitations list until then.

confirmed.theme: two functions that document themselves as mirroring each other's precondition checks actually check in a different order, so they can report a different *first* reason for the same invalid input
confirmed.summary: validateDetailed() (constraints.ts) checks structural validity (out-of-range constraint ids / self-pairs) BEFORE the size/work-budget checks and returns early on a structural hit. checkWellFormed() (constrainedGreedy.ts, the throw-based precondition for direct callers of constrainedGreedy) checks n/MAX_CONSTRAINED_N/k/MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK FIRST and only calls checkConstraintIds() (the structural mirror) afterward. The comment on checkConstraintIds says it is a 'Throw-on-first mirror of constraints.ts structuralReasons... keep the two checks in step' -- true for the id-validity logic in isolation, but the two entry points disagree on which class of problem is reported first when an input is both oversized AND structurally invalid.
confirmed.failure: n = 10000 (over MAX_CONSTRAINED_N = 5000) with a constraint pair referencing person 99999: validateDetailed(cons, k) returns [{code:'unknown-person', person:99999, n:10000}] (structural short-circuit fires before the n>MAX_CONSTRAINED_N check ever runs), while a direct call to constrainedGreedy(10000, k, cons) throws "roster size 10000 exceeds the constrained maximum of 5000" (checkWellFormed's n-cap check fires before checkConstraintIds runs). Same malformed input, two different 'first' diagnoses depending on which of the two documented-as-mirrored guards is asked.
confirmed.remediation: Reorder checkWellFormed to run checkConstraintIds before the size/k/work checks (matching validateDetailed's actual order), or state explicitly in both comments that only the *content* of the structural check is mirrored, not its priority relative to the size/work gates, so a future reader doesn't rely on 'in step' meaning identical precedence.
confirmed.invariant: for any (n, k, cons) that is both structurally invalid (out-of-range id or self-pair) and over a size/work cap, the Reason.code that would be first in validateDetailed(cons,k) matches the class of error thrown first by calling constrainedGreedy(n,k,cons) directly.

confirmed.theme: ambiguous constant relationship comment could mislead on whether values are identical
confirmed.summary: Comment claims UNVISITED is 'distinct from' UNREACHABLE but both are -1
confirmed.failure: Line 7 defines UNREACHABLE = -1; line 210 defines UNVISITED = -1 with comment 'distinct from bfsDistances' UNREACHABLE'. A maintainer reading 'distinct from' may assume they should have different values, then refactor them apart, breaking the logic. Both serve as visit-markers (same semantic function, different scopes) and sharing -1 is intentional and correct.
confirmed.invariant: When two constants in the same module share an identical value for valid semantic reasons, the comment must clarify the value reuse is intentional, not accidental. The word 'distinct' must not be used to describe a relationship where values are identical.
confirmed.remediation: Change the comment from 'distinct from bfsDistances' UNREACHABLE' to 'local redefinition of UNREACHABLE; same value (-1) but function-scoped', or 'per-source BFS marker; mirrors UNREACHABLE sentinel value'.

confirmed.theme: mixing original and promoted constraint references within same control flow breaks readability
confirmed.summary: Line 273 checks cons.priorCount; rest of buildConstrainedBuddyGraph (lines 259-282) consistently uses active
confirmed.failure: Function creates active = withHardPriors(cons) at line 259, then validates active (260), passes active to constrainedGreedy (263) and polishConstrained (276). But at line 273, deciding priorWeight, it checks cons.priorCount instead of active.priorCount. While functionally equivalent (active and cons have identical priors when priorHard is false), it breaks the local convention. A future maintainer modifying the promotion logic might assume the split reference is intentional and create a subtle bug.
confirmed.invariant: Within a single function where a promoted variant (active) is derived from an original (cons), references to the constraint set should use active consistently unless the comment explicitly justifies using the original.
confirmed.remediation: Change line 273 from 'cons.priorCount > 0' to 'active.priorCount > 0' for consistency with lines 260, 263, 271, 276.
